'''Frederick William Gehring'''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200604/comm-steele.pdf|title=Steele Prize award for Frederick Gehring}}</ref> (7 August 1925&nbsp;– 29 May 2012) was an American mathematician who worked in the area of [[complex analysis]]  ([[quasi-conformal mappings]]).

== Personal life ==

Both of Fred Gehring's parents graduated from the [[University of Michigan]].  His father, Carl Ernst Gehring, was a journalist who worked for the [[Ann Arbor News]] and a music critic.  His mother, Hester Reed Gehring, was a foreign language examiner for students who needed to prove competency as a requirement for their graduate degree.   She was also the daughter of [[John Oren Reed]], a physics professor and Dean of the College of Literature, Science and the Arts at the University of Michigan.

Gehring graduated from [[University High School (Michigan)|University High School]] in 1943 and hoped to attend the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].  However, because of [[World War II]], he was about to be drafted into the [[United States Navy]].  So he instead enrolled in the [[V-12 Navy College Training Program]] at the University of Michigan where he earned a BE in [[electrical engineering]] and a BA in [[mathematics]] in addition to completing various other Navy courses.  He finished his coursework close to [[Victory in Europe Day]].  After graduating, the Navy  sent him to serve on a [[destroyer]] in the [[Atlantic]] and [[Caribbean]].  When the war ended a few months later, Gehring was discharged from the Navy and returned to the University of Michigan, where he obtained a master's degree in mathematics.

In 1949, Gehring went to the [[University of Cambridge]] to study mathematics under [[John Charles Burkill]] at [[Peterhouse, Cambridge|Peterhouse]].  While there he met Lois Caroline Bigger, who was also working towards a Ph.D. (at [[Girton College]]).  Both were attending the University of Cambridge on [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright scholarships]].  Gehring received his [[Ph.D.]] in mathematics in 1952 while Lois Bigger received her Ph.D. three months earlier in [[biochemistry]].  They married one year after returning to the US on August 25, 1953, and have two sons, Kalle (born 21 December 1958) and Peter (born 29 September 1960).

== Career ==
Gehring served as a [[Benjamin Peirce]] instructor at [[Harvard University]] for three years after completing his doctoral work at the University of Cambridge.  In 1955 he returned to Ann Arbor, MI, to assume a post on the faculty of the Department of Mathematics at the [[University of Michigan]] where he worked until he retired at age 70.  During this time he supervised 29 Ph.D. students, six of whom are women, as well as 40 postdoctoral visitors.<ref>[http://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=7663 The Mathematics Genealogy Project]</ref>  He also served as chairman of the department on three separate occasions, serving for a total of eight years.

== Honors and awards ==

* 1986 – awarded the [[Order of the White Rose of Finland]], Commander class, Finland's highest scientific honor for foreigners.
* 1989 – elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].
* 1995 – awarded the [[Onsager Medal]].
*1997 – received an [[honorary degree]] (dr. philos. h.c.) from [[Norwegian University of Science and Technology|The Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ntnu.edu/phd/honorary-doctors|title=Honorary Doctors|website=www.ntnu.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-08-30}}</ref>
* 2006 – awarded the [[American Mathematical Society]] [[Steele Prize]] for Lifetime Achievement.

==Gehring's Lemma==
In a 1973 paper<ref name="Gehring1973">{{cite journal|last1=Gehring|first1=F. W.|title=The L<sup>p</sup>-integrability of the partial derivatives of a quasiconformal mapping|journal=Acta Mathematica|volume=130|year=1973|pages=265–277|issn=0001-5962|doi=10.1007/BF02392268|doi-access=free}}</ref> which has been cited over 800 times, Gehring proved the following lemma:<ref>{{cite arXiv|author=Maasalo, Outi Elina|title=The Gehring Lemma in Metric Spaces|year=2008|eprint=0704.3916|class=math.CA}}</ref><br>
Assume that <math>f</math> is a non–negative locally integrable function on {{math|R<sup>n</sup>}} and 1 < <math>p</math> < ∞. If there is a constant c<sub>1</sub> such that the inequality
::<math>\begin{align}&\left(\int_B |f(x)|^p\,dx\right)^{\frac{1}{p}} \end{align}</math> ≤ c<sub>1</sub><math>\begin{align}&\left(\int_B f(x)\,dx\right) \end{align}</math>
holds for all balls {{math|B}} of {{math|R<sup>n</sup>}}, then there exists <math>\varepsilon</math> > 0 and there exists a constant c<sub>2</sub> such that
::<math>\begin{align}&\left(\int_B |f(x)|^{p+\varepsilon}\,dx\right)^{\frac{1}{p+\varepsilon}} \end{align}</math> ≤ c<sub>2</sub><math>\begin{align}&\left(\int_B f(x)\,dx\right) \end{align}</math> holds for all balls {{math|B}} of {{math|R<sup>n</sup>}}.
